name: Vazquez v. County of Kern
court: Ninth Circuit (from the Eastern District of California, Magistrate Judge Jennifer L. Thurston)
topic: Staff sexual misconduct with a youth in custody, Fourteenth Amendment bodily privacy, bodily integrity, and punishment, qualified immunity, supervisory liability
summary: A 45-year-old male juvenile corrections officer at Kern County Juvenile Hall was accused of picking a girl in custody for work details so he could be alone with her, making sexual comments, touching her face and shoulders, telling her about a sexual dream, and watching her shower. The district court granted summary judgment to the officer and to his supervisor. The Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded. It held that, taking the evidence in the light most favorable to the youth, a reasonable jury could find violations of three Fourteenth Amendment rights; that the officer was not entitled to qualified immunity; and that a jury could find the supervisor "knew or reasonably should have known" of the violations "and failed to act to prevent them." The court also vacated the judgment in favor of the county and sent that part of the case back as well. The court did not find anyone liable. The case settled after remand and was dismissed with prejudice in September 2020.

No dissent or concurrence. Limits to keep in view: This was summary judgment. Every holding is framed as what "a jury could find" or "a reasonable jury could conclude" on the evidence viewed in the youth's favor. Anderson disputed key facts. The PREA training point rests on testimony that Anderson "likely" attended, from a trainer who "believed" he completed it and did not explain what the course covered. The PREA voyeurism definition the court quoted, "the inappropriate visual surveillance of a detainee for reasons unrelated to official duties," is cited to 6 C.F.R. section 115.6, which is the Department of Homeland Security's PREA rule (slip op. 19). The Department of Justice juvenile standards are in 28 C.F.R. Part 115, whose definition of voyeurism is worded differently. The opinion cites 28 C.F.R. section 115.6 for the definition of sexual harassment (slip op. 21 n.10). The opinion quotes York v. Story's reporter volume as "234 F.2d" in footnote 3 after citing it as 324 F.2d 450 in the text (slip op. 9). That inconsistency is in the opinion itself; it does not affect the holding.
facts:
The facts below are the evidence as the Ninth Circuit described it, viewed in the light most favorable to the youth because the case was decided on summary judgment. They are not findings that the events happened.

In January 2015, Samantha Vazquez was arrested on an outstanding warrant and taken to Kern County Juvenile Hall. She was housed in Unit 300A, an all-female unit, where Juvenile Corrections Officer George Anderson worked. Staff frequently placed wards on work "details," including laundry, kitchen, and clean-up (slip op. 4 to 5).

Vazquez testified that Anderson purposefully selected her to work details with him; called her "babe"; told her she had a "big butt" in the juvenile hall pants; "grabbed [her] face," "touched [her] shoulders," and talked with her about her shower gown. During one detail, she testified, he told her to shut the door, described a dream about her that was "rated R," then told her to get close to him "to the point where he had opened his knees and [she] was right in the middle of him," and said "that he wanted his dream to come true" (slip op. 5). She also alleged that he told her which shower stalls to use and looked at her inappropriately while she showered on three or four occasions, and that he told her he had seen her in the shower and that she should leave her boyfriend and "find someone better like him" (slip op. 6). The record showed that a person sitting at the staff counter in Unit 300A could see into at least one shower stall through a gap in the shower curtains (slip op. 6 n.2).

Vazquez first reported to a substance abuse specialist, who reported the allegations; the county opened an investigation the same day. The investigation lasted about eight months and included interviews of fifty-five people. The investigator testified that he "leaned toward them being true." The probation department's disciplinary review board sustained the allegations, and the county began the process of terminating Anderson's employment (slip op. 6).

Anderson testified that he selected Vazquez to work with him "once or twice," that "maybe once" they had been alone in a room for twenty minutes, that he chose her because she gave him gang intelligence and was a good worker, and that he remained at the staff counter while she showered on one or two occasions but was never told he could not sit there while female wards showered (slip op. 6 to 7). Several staff members testified that they saw Anderson alone with female wards, including Vazquez, and another testified she saw him at the staff counter while female wards showered (slip op. 7).

Hall policy at the time, as the director testified, included Section 1425 of the Juvenile Hall Basic Staff Rules: "Staff members are not permitted alone in the rooms with minors of the opposite gender except during an emergency. For security purposes, staff should avoid being alone with any minor in their room." The Juvenile Hall Administrative Manual required shower supervision by staff of the same gender as the youth (slip op. 7 to 8). The director also testified that standards in place at the time implemented the Prison Rape Elimination Act (slip op. 7).

The supervisor. Heathe Appleton was Anderson's supervisor. The opinion describes two things he knew (slip op. 22): He "observed Anderson alone with female wards on more than one occasion and failed to intervene." Anderson also testified that Appleton gave him permission to be alone in a cell with female wards during work details. The opinion does not give dates for these observations.

"Approximately six months before Vazquez raised her allegations," a staff member overheard Anderson tell a female ward to get ready to shower while the female staff and other wards were outside at physical education. She was concerned partly because of the gap in the shower curtains. "She took notes about the incident and reported it to Appleton."

The opinion describes Appleton's response this way: "Appleton did not write Anderson up, but he did bring up the incident with his supervisor." His supervisor told him to remind Anderson to have a female staff member in the unit during showers. Appleton testified that he did not recall exactly how he spoke to Anderson, but that he would have conveyed something "along the lines" of needing "to have a female present during showers" (slip op. 22). Appleton "was trained that if he observed any red flags of sexual abuse or if he received any reports from other staff members, he had to document and report the observations" (slip op. 22 n.11).

Procedural posture. Vazquez sued Anderson, Appleton, and the County of Kern under 42 U.S.C. section 1983, including municipal and supervisory liability claims. The district court granted summary judgment to Anderson and Appleton. It then ordered Vazquez to show cause whether the action could continue against the county; Vazquez, preserving her right to appeal, agreed it could not in light of those rulings, and the court dismissed the county and entered judgment for all defendants (slip op. 4 to 5 n.1).
holding:
Reversed and remanded. "The district court erred when it granted Anderson's and Appleton's motions for summary judgment. ... we REVERSE and REMAND for further proceedings consistent with this opinion" (slip op. 23). The court also vacated the cost award and "the district court's judgment in favor of Kern County and remand[ed] for further proceedings consistent with this opinion" (slip op. 23 n.12).

The officer: three constitutional claims go to a jury. "We hold that, viewing the facts in the light most favorable to Vazquez and drawing all reasonable inferences in her favor, she has presented sufficient facts to establish a violation of her right to bodily privacy, right to bodily integrity, and right to be free from punishment as guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment" (slip op. 9).

Bodily privacy. The court rejected Anderson's claimed security interest because "there is evidence in the record that his actions, at least with respect to the shower allegations, were against institution policy" (slip op. 11 to 12). Whether his viewing was "infrequent and casual" remained in dispute, and there was evidence he directed Vazquez to a stall "so he could obtain the best view" (slip op. 12). Holding: "a reasonable jury could conclude that Anderson violated Vazquez's Fourteenth Amendment right to bodily privacy" (slip op. 13).

Bodily integrity. Comparing the case to Fontana v. Haskin, the court stressed context: Vazquez "was a female ward at juvenile hall, whereas Anderson was 45 years old, was larger than Vazquez, wore a uniform, and had the power to discipline her if she refused to follow his instructions." A jury could find his conduct "was egregious and outrageous and shocks the conscience as a matter of law" (slip op. 15).

Freedom from punishment. Because Vazquez was a ward of the juvenile court, the claim was evaluated under the Fourteenth Amendment, not the Eighth. The district court erred by applying "the same standards" as an Eighth Amendment claim; the Fourteenth Amendment is more protective (slip op. 16 to 17). Holding: "a jury could find that Anderson violated Vazquez's Fourteenth Amendment right to be free from punishment" (slip op. 18).

Qualified immunity for the officer: denied. "We also hold that Anderson is not entitled to qualified immunity" (slip op. 9). The court stated that "Training materials and regulations are also relevant, although not dispositive, to determining whether reasonable officers would have been on notice that their conduct was unreasonable" (slip op. 19). It then rested the ruling on three sources of notice:

Bodily privacy. Clearly established law: "[i]t is clearly established that the Fourteenth Amendment protects a sphere of privacy, and the most 'basic subject of privacy . . . the naked body'" (slip op. 19, quoting Hydrick v. Hunter). Training: "Anderson also likely attended a PREA training." The PREA trainer "believed" Anderson and Appleton completed the training, and testified the course "goes over the policy," but "did not explicitly explain what was covered" (slip op. 19 and n.9). Policy: the hall required same-gender shower supervision. Conclusion: "given that we have clearly recognized a Fourteenth Amendment right to bodily privacy, the Juvenile Hall administrative policies, and the training Anderson likely attended, he is not entitled to qualified immunity for Vazquez's Fourteenth Amendment bodily privacy claim" (slip op. 20).

Bodily integrity and punishment. Anderson argued that his alleged sexual comments and contact were not equivalent to the sexual abuse the court had previously found unconstitutional. The court disagreed. Clearly established law: it relied on its own precedent, including Fontana v. Haskin, where it noted that similar conduct was "malum in se" and that "[n]o reasonable officer could believe that this conduct did not violate [the plaintiff's] constitutional rights" (slip op. 20). Policy and training: "the Kern County Juvenile Hall policy prohibiting staff members from being alone in a room with minors absent an emergency as well as Anderson's likely PREA training provided him with notice that his alleged conduct was unreasonable" (slip op. 20 to 21). Obviousness: "beyond the clearly established case law, training, and juvenile hall policies, it is 'obvious' that a juvenile corrections officer should not sexually harass or abuse a juvenile ward as it is always wrong for a juvenile corrections officer to engage in such conduct" (slip op. 21). Conclusion: "Accordingly, we conclude that Anderson is not entitled to qualified immunity for Vazquez's bodily integrity or punishment claims" (slip op. 21).

The supervisor: a triable claim. The court applied the rule that "a supervisor is liable for the acts of his subordinates if the supervisor participated in or directed the violations, or knew of the violations [of subordinates] and failed to act to prevent them," and that the causal connection can be shown "when an official sets in motion a series of acts by others which the actor knows or reasonably should know would cause others to inflict constitutional harms" (slip op. 21, quoting Preschooler II). On the two facts above, "a jury could find that Appleton knew or reasonably should have known of Anderson's violations and failed to act to prevent them," and "the district court erred when it concluded there was no evidence supporting a causal link between Appleton's conduct and Anderson's alleged violation of Vazquez's constitutional rights" (slip op. 22 to 23).

The county. The opinion vacated the judgment for Kern County and remanded (slip op. 23 n.12). That judgment had been entered only because Vazquez agreed, after the summary judgment rulings, that the claims against the county could not go forward in light of them (slip op. 4 to 5 n.1). The opinion contains no analysis of whether the county is liable.
notDecided:
Whether anything happened. No finding that Anderson did what was alleged, and no finding that Anderson, Appleton, or the county is liable.

The county's Monell liability. The court vacated the judgment for the county and remanded; it did not analyze or decide municipal liability.

Qualified immunity for the supervisor. The opinion's qualified immunity analysis is addressed to Anderson. The section on Appleton addresses only whether there was evidence of supervisory liability and causation; it does not discuss qualified immunity for Appleton.

The Fourth Amendment. The court addressed only the Fourteenth Amendment because Vazquez raised no Fourth Amendment argument on appeal (slip op. 13 n.6).

A more protective juvenile standard. The ACLU of Southern California argued as amicus that youth should get an even more protective standard than adult pretrial detainees. The court did "not address this argument because Vazquez can prevail under our existing Fourteenth Amendment standards" (slip op. 16 n.8).

Costs. Having reversed, the court did not consider the challenge to the cost award, and vacated the cost order (slip op. 23 and n.12).

What happened next. The case did not return to the Ninth Circuit. According to the district court's own orders, the parties filed a notice of settlement subject to approval by the Kern County Board of Supervisors, and the action was dismissed with prejudice in September 2020. No jury decided it.
inPractice:
For line staff in a juvenile facility: the cross-gender shower rule and the alone-with-a-youth rule are not paperwork. The court used them to defeat qualified immunity, both as evidence that the conduct served no legitimate purpose and as notice that the conduct was unreasonable.

Selecting one youth for work details so the two of you are alone is part of the record a jury hears, along with every comment about her body or clothing.

For supervisors: the theory against Appleton did not require that he participated. It rested on what he saw (an officer alone with female wards, and, according to the officer, permission to be alone in a cell with them during details) and what he was told (a staff member, who took notes about the incident, reported a shower incident to him approximately six months before Vazquez raised her allegations). His response was to raise the shower incident with his own supervisor and pass along a reminder, without writing the officer up, although he had been trained to document and report red flags and staff reports. On that record, the court held a jury could find he knew or reasonably should have known of the violations and failed to act to prevent them.

For agencies: written policy and PREA training cut both ways. They are evidence of what the institution expected, and they are evidence of what the individual officer and supervisor knew. Training records that show who attended and what was covered matter; in this case the court had to rely on a trainer's belief.
trainIt:
Teach the two hall rules from this case by name: no staff alone in a room with a youth of the opposite gender except in an emergency, and shower supervision by same-gender staff, with no opposite-gender viewing except in exigent circumstances or incidental to a routine safety check. Walk the unit and identify sight lines like the curtain gap in this case.

Teach grooming indicators as reportable: selecting one youth for isolated tasks, comments on body or clothing, physical touch, talk of personal relationships, and conversations about seeing a youth undressed.

Train supervisors that a staff report or an observed policy violation that touches sexual safety is a reportable event under agency PREA policy, not a coaching moment. Document what was reported, what was observed, what was done, and who was told. Route it through the PREA reporting chain and the agency's investigators, not only up the chain of command.

Train supervisors that permission matters. Authorizing an officer to be alone with youth of the opposite gender, contrary to policy, was part of the evidence against the supervisor here.

Build training records that prove attendance and content. Sign-in sheets, lesson plans, and test results answer the question the court could only answer with "likely."

Teach the posture correctly: this was a reversal of summary judgment that settled before trial. It is a case about what evidence gets a claim to a jury, not a verdict.

context.title: Related federal PREA standards (current text)
context.body: The Department of Justice PREA standards for juvenile facilities were not the basis of the court's ruling, but they address the same two subjects: staff reporting and cross-gender viewing. On reporting: "The agency shall require all staff to report immediately and according to agency policy any knowledge, suspicion, or information they receive regarding an incident of sexual abuse or sexual harassment that occurred in a facility," and "The agency shall also require all staff to comply with any applicable mandatory child abuse reporting laws" (28 C.F.R. section 115.361(a) and (b)). On cross-gender viewing: the facility must implement policies that enable residents to "shower, perform bodily functions, and change clothing without nonmedical staff of the opposite gender viewing their breasts, buttocks, or genitalia, except in exigent circumstances or when such viewing is incidental to routine cell checks" (28 C.F.R. section 115.315(d)).

context.title: Supreme Court cases the opinion relied on
context.body: As the Ninth Circuit described them, Bell v. Wolfish supplies the rule that pretrial detainees may not be punished, and Hope v. Pelzer is cited for considering a corrections regulation and a Department of Justice report in a qualified immunity analysis (slip op. 15 to 16, 19).

context.title: The California layer: mandated reporting
context.body:
No California Supreme Court or Court of Appeal decision applying Vazquez was verified for this brief. Vazquez is a federal constitutional case, but California law adds reporting duties that apply to the same facts in a California juvenile hall. These statutes were not discussed in the opinion. The text below is the current text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov.

Probation staff are mandated reporters. Penal Code section 11165.7, subdivision (a), lists as mandated reporters "(15) A social worker, probation officer, or parole officer," "(19) A peace officer, as defined in Chapter 4.5 (commencing with Section 830) of Title 3 of Part 2, who is not otherwise described in this section," and "(34) An employee of any police department, county sheriff's department, county probation department, or county welfare department."

The duty, the standard, and the clock. Penal Code section 11166, subdivision (a), requires a mandated reporter to report "whenever the mandated reporter, in the mandated reporter's professional capacity or within the scope of the mandated reporter's employment, has knowledge of or observes a child whom the mandated reporter knows or reasonably suspects has been the victim of child abuse or neglect." The initial report is made "by telephone to the agency immediately or as soon as is practicably possible," with "a written followup report within 36 hours of receiving the information concerning the incident." Reasonable suspicion "does not require certainty that child abuse or neglect has occurred" (section 11166, subd. (a)(1)). Failure to report is a misdemeanor (section 11166, subd. (c)).

Telling a supervisor is not a report. Section 11166, subdivision (i)(1): "The reporting duties under this section are individual, and no supervisor or administrator may impede or inhibit the reporting duties." Subdivision (i)(3): "Reporting the information regarding knowledge of or reasonably suspected child abuse or neglect to an employer, supervisor, school principal, school counselor, coworker, or other person shall not be a substitute for making a mandated report to an agency specified in Section 11165.9."

Abuse by institutional staff is covered. Penal Code section 11165.5 defines "abuse or neglect in out-of-home care" to include sexual abuse as defined in section 11165.1 "where the person responsible for the child's welfare is a licensee, administrator, or employee of any facility licensed to care for children, or an administrator or employee of a public or private school or other institution or agency." Section 11165.1 defines sexual abuse by reference to listed crimes, including "Section 647.6 (child molestation)." Whether particular conduct meets those definitions is a legal question for counsel and the receiving agency; the trigger for the reporter is reasonable suspicion.

A statute that does not fit this case. Penal Code section 289.6 criminalizes sexual activity by detention facility staff "with a consenting adult who is confined in a detention facility," and defines a detention facility as one "used for the confinement of adults or both adults and minors," among other places. By its terms it addresses confined adults. It should not be taught as the statute that governs staff conduct toward a minor in a juvenile-only hall.

applications.title: A red flag is a reportable event, not a coaching moment
applications.body: The supervisor in Vazquez had his own observations of the officer alone with female wards and a staff member's report, backed by her notes, about a shower incident. He did not write the officer up; he raised the shower incident with his own supervisor and passed along a reminder to have a female present during showers. On that record, the court held a jury could find he knew or reasonably should have known of the violations and failed to act to prevent them. Document it, report it through the PREA chain, and act on it.

applications.title: Policy is notice
applications.body: The court used the hall's alone-with-a-youth rule, its same-gender shower rule, and PREA training to deny qualified immunity. If the policy exists, staff will be held to it, and so will the people who supervise them.

applications.title: Supervisors cannot authorize around the rule
applications.body: Testimony that the supervisor gave permission to be alone in a cell with female wards during work details was part of the supervisory case.

applications.title: In California, telling your supervisor is not the report
applications.body: Under Penal Code section 11166, subdivision (i)(3), an internal report does not substitute for a mandated report when there is reasonable suspicion of child abuse. Train both duties: the PREA report inside the agency and the mandated report outside it.

applications.title: Prove the training
applications.body: "Likely attended" was enough for the court here, but it is not what an agency wants to rely on. Keep attendance and content records.

applications.title: Teach the posture accurately
applications.body: Vazquez reversed summary judgment and sent the case back. It did not find the officer, the supervisor, or the county liable, and it did not decide the county's liability. The case then settled.

quiz.q: What did the Ninth Circuit decide about the supervisor in Vazquez v. County of Kern?
options: It found him personally liable and awarded damages
It held a jury could find he knew or reasonably should have known of the officer's violations and failed to act to prevent them, so summary judgment was reversed
It granted him qualified immunity because he reported the incident to his own supervisor
It held supervisors are liable for everything their subordinates do
quiz.teach: There is no pure respondeat superior liability under section 1983. The claim survived because of what the supervisor saw and was told, and how he responded. It was sent back for further proceedings, not decided.

quiz.q: On what basis did the court deny the officer qualified immunity on the bodily privacy claim?
options: Only because the youth was a minor
Because the county began the process of terminating the officer
The clearly recognized Fourteenth Amendment right to bodily privacy, the juvenile hall administrative policies, and the PREA training he likely attended
Because PREA creates a private right to sue
quiz.teach: The court said training materials and regulations are relevant, though not dispositive, to whether officers were on notice. Policy and training became part of the qualified immunity analysis.

quiz.q: What did the Ninth Circuit do with the judgment in favor of Kern County?
options: Affirmed it, because counties are never liable for staff misconduct
Held the county liable under Monell
Vacated it and remanded for further proceedings, without deciding the county's liability
quiz.teach: The county judgment had been entered only because the claims against the county could not go forward after the summary judgment rulings. Once those rulings were reversed, the county judgment was vacated too. Municipal liability was left for remand.
